content: Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) in children is defined by partial or complete obstruction of the upper airway during sleep. It affects approximately 1% to 4% of children, with adenotonsillar hypertrophy being the most common underlying risk factor. The current first-line treatment for OSA caused by adenotonsillar hypertrophy is surgical removal of the adenoids or tonsils. However, surgery carries perioperative risks and has a recurrence rate of up to 20%, prompting interest in less invasive alternatives. Since enlarged adenoids and tonsils are composed of hypertrophied lymphoid tissue, anti-inflammatory medications have been proposed as a potential non-surgical treatment option for children with OSA. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of anti-inflammatory drugs in treating OSA in children. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing anti-inflammatory drugs to placebo in children aged 1 to 16 years with objectively diagnosed OSA (apnoea/hypopnoea index (AHI) ≥ 1 per hour) were included. The primary outcomes assessed were AHI and serious adverse events. Secondary outcomes included measures such as the respiratory disturbance index, desaturation index, respiratory arousal index, nadir arterial oxygen saturation, mean arterial oxygen saturation, avoidance of surgical treatment, clinical symptom scores, tonsillar size, and adverse events. Five trials involving 240 children aged 1 to 18 years with mild to moderate OSA (AHI 1 to 30 per hour) were included. These trials were conducted in specialised sleep medicine clinics at tertiary care centres, with follow-up periods ranging from six weeks to four months. Three RCTs (137 participants) compared intranasal corticosteroids to placebo, while two RCTs (103 participants) compared oral montelukast to placebo. One trial was excluded from the meta-analysis due to improper randomisation analysis, and selective reporting was a concern in another trial. For intranasal corticosteroids, the evidence for a difference in AHI compared to placebo was uncertain (mean difference (MD) −3.18, 95% confidence interval (CI) −8.70 to 2.35; low-certainty evidence). Secondary outcomes such as the desaturation index (MD −2.12, 95% CI −4.27 to 0.04; moderate-certainty evidence), respiratory arousal index (MD −0.71, 95% CI −6.25 to 4.83; low-certainty evidence), and nadir oxygen saturation (MD 0.59%, 95% CI −1.09 to 2.27; moderate-certainty evidence) also showed uncertain results. For oral montelukast, children had a significantly lower AHI compared to placebo (MD −3.41, 95% CI −5.36 to −1.45; moderate-certainty evidence). Montelukast also reduced the respiratory arousal index (MD −2.89, 95% CI −4.68 to −1.10; moderate-certainty evidence) and improved nadir oxygen saturation (MD 4.07%, 95% CI 2.27 to 5.88; high-certainty evidence). However, the difference in the desaturation index between montelukast and placebo was uncertain (MD −2.50, 95% CI −5.53 to 0.54; low-certainty evidence). Adverse events were rare, minor (e.g., nasal bleeding), and evenly distributed between study groups. None of the included studies evaluated the avoidance of surgical treatment for OSA as an outcome. In conclusion, there is insufficient evidence to support the efficacy of intranasal corticosteroids for treating OSA in children. While they may have short-term benefits on the desaturation index and oxygen saturation in children with mild to moderate OSA, the certainty of their effect on AHI and the respiratory arousal index is low due to imprecise estimates and study heterogeneity. Montelukast demonstrated short-term benefits in reducing apnoeas, hypopnoeas, and respiratory arousals during sleep in otherwise healthy, non-obese, surgically untreated children. It was well tolerated, with moderate to high certainty for some outcomes. However, the clinical significance of these findings remains unclear, as minimal clinically important differences for polysomnography-based outcomes in children have not been established. Long-term efficacy and safety data for anti-inflammatory medications in treating childhood OSA are lacking. Additionally, patient-centred outcomes such as concentration ability, vigilance, or school performance have not been studied. No RCTs have been conducted on other types of anti-inflammatory medications for OSA in children. Future RCTs should focus on the sustainability of treatment effects, avoidance of surgical interventions, long-term safety, and patient-centred outcomes.
